body:
Taking the account, objection, and rival together, the most defensible move is not to choose between the memory-gap reading and the avoidance-as-central reading, but to run a low-cost probe that could discriminate between them, and to treat every remedy as conditional on what that probe returns. The rival's probe—asking each flatmate separately what they thought a past agreement meant—is the right first step, but I would broaden it slightly: ask each person, individually, what they thought a past agreement meant and what they think keeps going wrong in the group conversations. Frame it as wanting to hear their view, not as asking why they avoid (the rival's framing point). This is not a truth-finding exercise; it is a way to see whether the later disagreements cluster around scope (what task), recurrence (how often), or timing (by when), or whether they point instead at standing, fairness, or being unheard. The clustering is the discriminating observation the rival proposed. It gives current reports, not ground truth, and it can be read as interrogation, so it can fail. If it fails, that is information about the cost of the probe, not evidence for any reading.

If the reports cluster around scope, recurrence, or timing, the narrowest next step is the rival's second reading: state scope out loud at the moment of agreement—'when I say I'll do the dishes this week, I mean these tasks, this week, and then we re-agree.' That is a practice, not a record, and it directly addresses the ambiguity that a record alone would not settle (the objection's memorial/normative distinction). If the reports do not cluster, or if they point to standing or being unheard, then the group conversation should be about how the group talks, not about chores—naming the pattern without blame, as the objection's avoidance-as-central reading suggests. In that case the account's separate approach to the avoidant friend is still relevant, but it should be reframed as the rival proposes: 'I want to hear your view of the group conversations,' not 'I want to ask why you avoid them.' And the rival's warning stands: if the friend experiences the private conversation as reproducing the outnumbered dynamic, that counts against the approach.

Only after that would I consider a shared note or a weekly check-in. Treat either as an experiment, not a fix. If a note is tried, pair it with explicit scope statements at the moment of agreement, and watch for two failure modes the prior pieces name: the argument relocating onto the note (who wrote it, who is on it, what it covers) and the note being read as surveillance by the person who withdrew. The account's own caveat about the check-in assuming all three can talk without a mediator is not peripheral; it is a reason to make the check-in conditional and small, and to be willing to drop it if it becomes another chore. The objection's sharpened test is worth adopting: if a record is tried and 'done' is defined and the recurring arguments continue or intensify, that counts against the memory-gap-as-central reading and for the avoidance-as-central or standing-negotiation readings.

What I reject: the account's diagnostic confidence that the memory gap is the central mechanism, and the slide from 'no shared record' to 'make a shared record' as if the diagnosis were established. I also reject the idea that a written record alone resolves what 'done' or 'this week' should mean; that is a normative question, as the objection says. I do not reject the possibility that a record helps if paired with explicit scope statements. I also do not accept the account's presentation of the one-to-one approach as clearly correct; the rival's criticism that it may reproduce the same dynamic at smaller scale is well taken. But I also do not accept the objection's implicit ranking if it treats the approach as clearly the load-bearing move independent of framing; the framing matters, and the probe may show that neither the record nor the approach is the right first move.

What stays open: whether the household wants any formalization; whether the avoidant friend's withdrawal is recent or long-standing; whether the load is unequal; whether the disagreements are symmetric; whether a mediator or a different division of labor would be better. Nothing in the material lets me rank those. The original problem asks what to do. My answer is: start with the probe, let the clustering guide the next step, keep the record and check-in conditional, reframe the individual conversation, and report back what the household actually says. That is a commitment to further inquiry, not to a diagnosis or a remedy.
commitments: Taking this up involves running the rival's probe in the broadened form I described, and treating the resulting reports as current interpretations, not as ground truth about what was agreed. It means holding the memory-gap, scope-ambiguity, and standing-negotiation readings as live alternatives, and not using the probe to confirm whichever one is already preferred. It means treating any written record or weekly check-in as a conditional experiment, to be paired with explicit scope statements and watched for relocation onto the record and for surveillance effects. It means reframing the private conversation with the avoidant friend as hearing their view of the group, and being alert to the rival's warning that a private approach can reproduce the outnumbered dynamic. It means adopting the objection's sharpened test: if a record is tried and arguments continue, that counts against the memory-gap-as-central reading. It means not committing to a mediator, a chore reassignment, or formalization, but leaving them open. It means acknowledging the unresolved gaps: no ground truth about past agreements, no data on load distribution, no history of the avoidance, no assurance that all three can talk without a mediator. It means reporting back what the household actually says rather than what fits a preferred reading. The commitment is to further inquiry and a local trial, not to the truth of any diagnosis or the success of any intervention. If the probe is experienced as interrogation, or if the avoidant friend will not talk one-to-one, that outcome should count against the probe's value, not be explained away. If the reports do not cluster, that should weaken the memory-gap reading rather than be treated as inconclusive in a way that protects it.
